chapters.title: Principles
chapters.intro: Before pixels: know what the page is for. Every screen should answer three questions in about five seconds: what is this, what can I do here, and why should I care?

rules.do: Give each screen one primary action and make it visually obvious.
rules.dont: Give five buttons equal weight and make people work out which one matters.
rules.why: When everything is emphasized, nothing is. Hierarchy is how a design tells people where to look.

rules.do: Use conventions people already know: logo top-left links home, search looks like search, links look like links.
rules.dont: Reinvent scrolling, navigation or form controls for novelty.
rules.why: People spend most of their time on other sites (Jakob’s Law). Familiar patterns cost them nothing to learn.

rules.do: Remove things until the page breaks, then put the last one back.
rules.dont: Fill space because it’s empty. Whitespace is a feature, not waste.

rules.do: Be consistent: the same thing should look and behave the same everywhere.
rules.dont: Use three button styles, four greys and two date formats for the same job.
rules.why: A design system (even a small one, like our tokens file) is how you stay consistent without thinking about it.

chapters.title: Layout & spacing
chapters.intro: Spacing is the quietest design tool and the one that most separates amateur from professional work. Pick a scale and stick to it.

rules.do: Use a spacing scale based on 4 or 8: 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96.
rules.dont: Pick values by eye: 13px here, 17px there, 22px somewhere else. It reads as messy even when nobody can say why.

rules.do: Put related things close together and unrelated things further apart. A label sits closer to its field than to the field above.
rules.dont: Space everything evenly. Equal gaps erase the grouping people use to read a page.
rules.why: This is the law of proximity: distance is how the eye decides what belongs together.

rules.do: Keep body text between 45 and 75 characters per line. max-width: 65ch does it in one line of CSS.
rules.dont: Let paragraphs stretch the full width of a 1440px screen. Long lines make readers lose their place.

rules.do: Align to a grid and left-align body text (right-align in right-to-left languages).
rules.dont: Center-align long paragraphs. Every line starts in a different place, so reading is slower.

chapters.title: Typography
chapters.intro: Most of the web is text. Get type right and a plain design looks considered; get it wrong and no amount of decoration helps.

rules.do: Use at least 16px for body text with a line height of 1.5 to 1.7.
rules.dont: Set body text at 12–13px in light grey. It looks elegant in a mockup and is unreadable on a phone in sunlight.

rules.do: Use a type scale with a fixed ratio (for example 1.25: 16, 20, 25, 31, 39, 49) and at most two typefaces.
rules.dont: Use five fonts and a dozen sizes picked one at a time.

rules.do: Build hierarchy with size, weight and color, and use each sparingly. Headings should be clearly bigger than text, not 2px bigger.
rules.dont: Bold whole paragraphs or write sentences in ALL CAPS. Emphasis everywhere is emphasis nowhere.

rules.do: Use one <h1> per page and keep heading levels in order (h2 then h3, never skipping).
rules.dont: Pick heading tags for their default size. Style with CSS; choose the tag for meaning.
rules.why: Screen-reader users jump between headings to navigate. Search engines use them to understand the page.

rules.do: Load web fonts carefully: two or three weights, font-display: swap, WOFF2, self-hosted where you can. System fonts are a perfectly good choice.
rules.dont: Load a font family in nine weights to use two of them.

chapters.title: Color & contrast
chapters.intro: Color carries meaning and mood, but its first job is legibility. Contrast is measurable, so measure it.

rules.do: Check every text and background pair against those numbers.
rules.dont: Use pale grey text on white to look “minimal”.

rules.do: Keep a small palette: neutrals, one accent, and semantic colors for success, warning and danger.
rules.dont: Use your accent color for decoration and for clickable things. If blue means “click”, only clickable things are blue.

rules.do: Pair color with a second cue: an icon, a label, an underline, a pattern.
rules.dont: Show status with a red or green dot alone. About 1 in 12 men can’t reliably tell them apart.

rules.do: Design dark mode on purpose: dark grey backgrounds (not pure black), slightly softer text, and lighter, less saturated accents.
rules.dont: Invert your light theme and call it done. Shadows vanish, colors vibrate and white text on pure black glares.

chapters.title: Buttons & links
chapters.intro: A button does something. A link goes somewhere. Keeping that distinction clear fixes a surprising number of usability and accessibility problems.

rules.do: Show a clear hierarchy: one primary, then secondary, then text links.
rules.dont: Make every option a loud, filled button.

rules.do: Start labels with a verb that says what happens: “Save changes”, “Download invoice”, “Delete project”.
rules.dont: Write “Submit”, “OK”, “Yes” or “Click here”. Out of context (and screen readers often list links out of context) they mean nothing.

rules.do: Use <button> for actions and <a href> for navigation.
rules.dont: Put a click handler on a <div>. It can’t be focused, doesn’t respond to Enter or Space, and isn’t announced as a button.

rules.do: Make touch targets at least 44 × 44px, with space between them. (WCAG 2.2 sets an absolute floor of 24 × 24.)
rules.dont: Cram tiny icon buttons together so people tap the wrong one.

rules.do: Show a loading state on click and block double submits. For destructive actions, confirm with a specific label or, better, offer Undo.
rules.dont: Leave a button looking idle while a request runs, so people click it three more times.

chapters.title: Forms
chapters.intro: Forms are where users give you something: money, data, trust. Every extra field and every unclear error costs you completions.

rules.do: Put a visible label above every field.
rules.dont: Use the placeholder as the label. It disappears the moment someone starts typing.

rules.do: Show errors next to the field, in words that say how to fix it.
rules.dont: Show “Invalid input” in a banner at the top, or clear the form when something is wrong.

rules.do: Use the right input types and autocomplete values (type="email", autocomplete="one-time-code") so phones show the right keyboard and browsers can fill things in.
rules.dont: Ask for things you don’t need. Every optional field is a reason to leave.

rules.do: Lay forms out in a single column, and validate when a field loses focus or on submit.
rules.dont: Shout an error after the first keystroke, before the person has had a chance to finish.

rules.do: Accept input in the forms people use: spaces in card numbers, dashes in phone numbers, any capitalization in email addresses.
rules.dont: Disable paste in password or email fields. It punishes password managers and makes accounts less secure.

chapters.title: Navigation
chapters.intro: Navigation answers “where am I, and where can I go?” If people have to think about it, it isn’t working.

rules.do: Keep top-level navigation to about five to seven items with plain names (“Pricing”, “Docs”, “Contact”).
rules.dont: Use clever labels like “Discover”, “Solutions” or “Our world” that could mean anything.

rules.do: Show where people are: highlight the current section and set aria-current="page". Add breadcrumbs on deep sites.
rules.dont: Hide navigation behind a hamburger icon on desktop when there’s room to show it.

rules.do: Make links look like links (underlines in body text are good), and keep URLs readable and shareable.
rules.dont: Open links in new tabs by default. Let people choose; the back button is the most-used control on the web.

chapters.title: Accessibility
chapters.intro: About one in six people has a disability, and everyone is temporarily impaired sometimes: a broken arm, bright sunlight, a slow connection. Accessible design is simply design that works.

rules.do: Make everything work with a keyboard alone, in a logical tab order, with a clearly visible focus state (:focus-visible).
rules.dont: Write outline: none without a replacement, or use positive tabindex values.

rules.do: Write alt text that says what an image is for (“Chart: sign-ups doubled in March”). Use alt="" for purely decorative images.
rules.dont: Write “image of…”, repeat the file name, or leave alt off entirely (screen readers then read the file name aloud).

rules.do: Support 200% zoom and a 320px-wide viewport without sideways scrolling. Set lang on <html> and a unique <title> per page.
rules.dont: Disable pinch zoom with maximum-scale=1 or user-scalable=no.

rules.do: Add a “Skip to content” link, use landmarks (header, nav, main, footer) and announce dynamic updates with live regions.
rules.dont: Rely on hover alone, or on time limits people can’t extend.
rules.why: Test it: unplug your mouse for five minutes, then try your page with a screen reader (VoiceOver on Mac/iOS, NVDA on Windows, TalkBack on Android).

chapters.title: Feedback & states
chapters.intro: Mockups show the happy path. Real products spend a lot of time in the other states. Design all of them.

rules.do: Respond to every action within about 100ms, even if only by showing that the click registered.
rules.dont: Let a click do nothing visible while the network catches up.

rules.do: Write errors like a helpful person: “That card was declined. Try another card or contact your bank.”
rules.dont: Show “Error 0x80004005” or “Something went wrong” with no way forward.

chapters.title: Motion
chapters.intro: Good motion explains: where something came from, where it went, what changed. Bad motion performs.

rules.do: Keep UI transitions between 150 and 300ms. Use ease-out for things entering and ease-in for things leaving.
rules.dont: Make people wait for a 1-second animation before they can click.

rules.do: Animate transform and opacity, which the browser can animate smoothly.
rules.dont: Animate width, height, top or left, which force layout on every frame and stutter on slower phones.

rules.do: Honor prefers-reduced-motion: replace slides and parallax with simple fades or nothing.
rules.dont: Autoplay carousels or background video with no pause control. They distract, and for some people cause nausea.

chapters.title: Responsive design
chapters.intro: Most visits come from phones. Design for the small screen first and let the layout grow, rather than squeezing a desktop page down.

rules.do: Set breakpoints where your content breaks, and use fluid sizing like clamp(2rem, 5vw, 4rem) for headings.
rules.dont: Design for specific devices (“iPhone 15 width”). Next year’s devices will be different.

rules.do: Keep key actions within thumb reach on phones and test on a real device, not just a resized browser.
rules.dont: Hide important content or features on mobile. People on phones want the same things.

rules.do: Use relative units (rem, %, ch) and modern layout (flexbox, grid, container queries).
rules.dont: Fix heights on text containers. Translations, zoom and real content will overflow them.

chapters.title: Performance
chapters.intro: Speed is a design feature. A beautiful page that takes six seconds to load is, for most visitors, a blank page.

rules.do: Serve images in AVIF or WebP at the size they’re shown, with width and height set and loading="lazy" below the fold.
rules.dont: Ship a 4MB PNG hero image, or images without dimensions that shove the text down as they load.

rules.do: Ship less JavaScript. Reach for HTML and CSS first; many components here need no JS at all.
rules.dont: Add a library for something the platform already does (<dialog>, <details>, form validation, smooth scrolling).

chapters.title: Content & ethics
chapters.intro: Words are interface. And trust, once spent on a trick, doesn’t come back.

rules.do: Write like a person. Put the important words first, keep sentences short, and use headings and lists so pages can be scanned.
rules.dont: Write walls of text full of jargon (“Leverage our synergistic platform”).

rules.do: Make cancelling as easy as signing up, show the full price up front, and make the privacy-friendly choice the default.
rules.dont: Use dark patterns: pre-ticked opt-ins, hidden fees, fake countdown timers, or confirmshaming (“No thanks, I don’t like saving money”).
rules.why: Beyond being wrong, many of these are now illegal in the EU, UK and parts of the US.

rules.do: Ask for permissions (notifications, location) at the moment they’re needed and say why.
rules.dont: Fire a cookie banner, a newsletter pop-up and a notification prompt in the first three seconds.

chapters.title: Pre-launch checklist
chapters.intro: Run through this before you ship. Your progress is saved in this browser.
checklist: Each page has one clear purpose and one primary action.
All text passes 4.5:1 contrast (3:1 for large text and UI parts).
Everything works with a keyboard, and focus is always visible.
One h1 per page; headings are in order.
Every meaningful image has alt text; decorative ones have alt="".
Every form field has a visible label and helpful error messages.
Tested on a real phone, at 320px wide and at 200% zoom.
Empty, loading, error and success states are designed.
Images are compressed, sized, and have width/height set.
Lighthouse / PageSpeed shows good Core Web Vitals.
Every page has a unique title, meta description and lang attribute.
No broken links; the 404 page helps people find their way.
Buttons say what they do; copy has been read aloud once.
No dark patterns: pricing is clear, opting out is easy.
